INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Infeed Jam), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv – three underfill alarms recorded on night shift 2026‑09‑10
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv – line stopped at 04:45 on 2026‑09‑10 due to worn seals
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑26‑Night.csv – no prior underfill alarms recorded
- FL-101‑SOP.txt Rev 1.0 – Section 6.1 (PPE), Section 6.2 (LOTO), Section 6.3‑6.4 (Machine safety rules), Section 12.1 (Underfill alarm response), pre‑start checklist
- FL-101‑Work‑Instruction.txt – seal replacement procedure (WI‑FL101‑001)
- Knowledge‑graph entry – LOTO (SAF‑003) mandatory for any maintenance or restart
- Knowledge‑graph entry – Machine safety rules: never clear jam while running, never reach past guard, never bypass guard switches
- Expert Fix Agent – NO prior expert fix record (NO DATA)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: worn fill‑valve seals caused valve drip on valves 9, 15 and newly valve 3, producing three consecutive underfill alarms after the line had been idle since Friday night.
- Difference from historical pattern: previous underfill events involved only valves 9 and 15 and occurred briefly; this incident adds valve 3 and follows an extended idle period with documented worn seals, indicating a more severe seal failure.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped; no product output since Friday night, risk of extended downtime.
- Safety risk: HIGH (LOTO required, machine stop, potential for fluid leakage or bottle breakage).
- Financial impact: not quantified in provided data, but loss of production time and potential scrap from underfilled bottles.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms in one shift and a required LOTO for seal replacement meet the HIGH minimum per criticality rules.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action
  Step 1: Safety — Apply LOTO per SAF‑003: shut off power at the main isolator, place personal lock, tag with name and date.
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Inspect fill‑valve seals on valves 9, 15, and 3 for wear or damage; verify that no fluid is leaking onto the floor.
  Step 3: Fix — Replace the worn seals following WI‑FL101‑001; re‑install seals ensuring proper seating; tighten according to the work instruction.
  Step 4: Verify — Remove LOTO, power the line, run a test fill at 60 bpm for two minutes, monitor the checkweigher for underfill; confirm no alarm after three consecutive bottles.
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced during the alarm period; inspect for underfill and reject non‑conforming product.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution)
  • Implement a scheduled seal inspection and replacement program for all fill valves after any idle period exceeding 24 hours.

- Preventive action (stops recurrence)
  • Add a pre‑start checklist item to verify seal condition and valve drip before restarting after an idle period.
  • Log seal condition in the shift change record; trigger maintenance ticket if any seal shows wear.
  • Train operators on the expanded valve‑drip symptom (including valve 3) and reinforce LOTO compliance.

- Who to notify
  • Maintenance Supervisor
  • Shift Lead
  • Quality Lead
  • Production Planner

═══════════════════════════════════════
PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

SITUATION: The filling line has been idle since Friday night and now shows three underfill alarms due to worn valve seals.
ROOT CAUSE: Worn fill‑valve seals allowed valve drip, causing underfill after an extended idle period.
STATUS: Line is stopped pending seal replacement and LOTO.
ACTION REQUIRED: Apply LOTO, replace the worn seals on all affected fill valves, and run a test fill before restarting.
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued production loss, potential for product quality failures, and safety exposure from uncontrolled fluid leaks.

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Infeed Jam  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
  safety rule: Never reach into the infeed or the star wheel while the machine is running. Stop the machine and lock it out before clearing any jam.
  alarm message: Infeed jam — bottles stopped at infeed
  if a bottle breaks: If a bottle breaks during a jam, stop and follow SOP Section 12.3.
  first check: If a changeover happened this shift, check the changeover record first.
  causes in order: 1. Guide rails not reset after a bottle size changeover. 2. Chipped or damaged bottles. 3. Bottle feed conveyor running too fast.
  SPECIFICATION — Guide Rail Setting: reference: Changeover sheet CS-FL101; bottle 500 ml: Rail position A; bottle 330 ml: Rail position B; also check: Rails locked and the matching star wheel fitted  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2 and 14]
  SPECIFICATION — Line Speed: normal: 120 bottles per minute (maximum 130); start: Start at 60 bottles per minute, then raise to normal speed once the first bottles are in range  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 9 and 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Guide Rails Not Reset After Changeover  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2, 12.2 and 14]
        note: Most infeed jams in the first hour after a changeover come from rails left in the wrong position
        check: Check the guide rail position matches the bottle size, and that the rails are locked
        fix: Bottle Size Changeover  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 14]
            steps: 1. Lock out the machine. 2. Move the guide rails to the position on changeover sheet CS-FL101 and lock them. 3. Fit the matching star wheel. 4. Remove the lock and run 20 bottles at 60 bottles per minute. 5. Check none jam and all fill correctly, then return to normal speed. 6. Record the changeover in the shift log; the shift lead signs the changeover record.
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
    - Chipped or Damaged Bottles  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
        fix: Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed, wearing cut-resistant gloves
        fix: Infeed Jam Clearing  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
            steps: 1. Press STOP. 2. Lock out the machine. 3. Remove the jammed bottles wearing cut-resistant gloves. 4. Check the guide rail position matches the bottle size, and reset the rails if they are wrong. 5. Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed. 6. Remove the lock, restart at 60 bottles per minute for 2 minutes, then return to normal speed.
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Bottle Feed Conveyor Running Too Fast  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
        note: Third most common cause of infeed jams. The SOP gives no specific fix for it.
  procedure: Infeed Jam Clearing (details above)
  procedure: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 13]
      electrical rule: Do not attempt electrical repairs. Always call maintenance.

Applies to all 24 fill valves on the FL-101 Bottle Filler. Only trained

3. WHEN TO REPLACE THE SEALS

Replace the seal kit when:

  - The checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again
  - Three or more underfill alarms happen in one shift
  - The seal has reached its limit: 3 months or 1,500 running hours,
    whichever comes first

  A typical job (1 to 4 valves): 30 to 45 minutes

  Food-grade lubricant:     FGL-1
  Location:                 Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2

Alarm message: "Fill level low — bottles under target volume"
The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row.

  3. Low product supply pressure — see Section 12.4

  - Safety glasses at all times
  - Cut-resistant gloves when handling glass or change parts
  - Hearing protection

LOTO is required before any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or

  3. Tag it with your name and the date.

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: worn valve seals leaked after the line sat idle since Friday night, causing low fill volume and three consecutive underfill alarms on the night shift of 10 Sep 2026. (Evidence: alarm pattern, stop due to worn seals, no maintenance record)
- Difference vs historical pattern: this is the first recorded underfill event; previously no underfill alarms appear in the provided logs and no expert fix exists.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line remains stopped; no bottles are being filled.
- Safety risk: HIGH – LOTO is required for seal inspection/replacement; guard rules must be observed to prevent injury.
- Financial impact: loss of production since Friday night plus potential scrap of underfilled bottles; exact dollar amount not quantified in the data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms in one shift and a required production stop trigger the HIGH rating per the criticality rules.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action
  Step 1: Safety — LOTO the filler (switch off power at main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start) [source: FL‑101‑SOP Section 6.2].
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Wear protective glasses, cut‑resistant gloves, hearing protection, safety shoes; open guard doors and inspect valve 9, valve 15, and valve 3 for seal condition and leakage.
  Step 3: Fix — Replace any worn seals following WI‑FL101‑001 seal‑replacement procedure; re‑tighten valve connections per the work instruction.
  Step 4: Verify — Restart the line at 60 bottles/min, run at least 20 bottles, confirm fill level meets target; monitor for further underfill alarms.
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced after restart until fill verification is complete; inspect for underfill and reject non‑conforming units.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution)
  • Replace all valve seals on Filling Line 1 as part of a scheduled maintenance task after any shutdown longer than 12 hours.
  • Update the work instruction to include a “post‑idle seal inspection” checklist.

- Preventive action (stops recurrence)
  • Add a SOP section that defines the restart procedure after an extended idle period, mandating seal inspection, LOTO, and a low‑speed trial run.
  • Train operators on the new restart checklist and reinforce guard and LOTO compliance.
  • Log all seal inspections in the shift handover record to create a maintenance history.

- Who to notify
  • Maintenance Supervisor
  • Shift Lead
  • Quality Lead
  • Plant Manager

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: worn or damaged fill‑valve seals (and possible debris) causing valve drip and underfill alarms after the line was restarted following a prior seal‑wear stoppage.
- Difference from historical pattern: this is the first recorded instance of underfill alarms on Filling Line 1; previously no underfill events were logged, indicating a new mechanical fault rather than a recurring operational issue.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped for worn seals, then underfill alarms prevented restart; line currently idle.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO and PPE; fault triggers repeated alarms and could lead to product contamination if not addressed).
- Financial impact: loss of production time since Friday night and potential scrap of underfilled bottles; exact cost not quantified in provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms occurred in a single shift, meeting the HIGH minimum for recurring faults and requiring LOTO for inspection.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Perform LOTO per SAF‑003: switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start.
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Inspect fill‑valve seals and nozzle for wear or debris; inspect valves 9, 15, 3 for dripping; verify product supply pressure is within normal limits (SOP Section 12.4).
  Step 3: Fix — Replace any worn seals; clean or replace leaking valve components; ensure guard doors are closed and safety switches functional; wear required PPE (safety glasses, cut‑resistant gloves, hearing protection, safety shoes).
  Step 4: Verify — Run a test fill; confirm the checkweigher registers fewer than 3 consecutive underfilled bottles; observe for any further underfill alarms.
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced during the alarm period; inspect for underfill and reject as per quality procedure.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Implement a post‑idle seal inspection and replacement schedule; update the preventive maintenance plan to include seal checks after any shutdown longer than 12 hours.
- Preventive action: Add “inspect fill‑valve seals and nozzle” to the pre‑start checklist; train operators on the added step; log seal inspections in the shift record; review alarm trends weekly.
- Who to notify: Maintenance Supervisor, Shift Lead, Quality Lead, and Production Control.

SOURCE DATA:

- FL‑101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections on alarm response, underfill procedure, product supply pressure, safety steps, specifications
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt – NCR‑2026‑012 (underfill alarms caused by worn seals on valve 12, corrective action completed)
- FL‑101‑Work-Instruction.txt – cause note: blocked nozzle may produce underfill without drips
- Knowledge‑graph for FL‑101 (Tier 1 verified) – fault definition, cause hierarchy, correct response, specifications, mandatory safety rules
- WI‑FL101‑001 (referenced in knowledge graph) – seal‑replacement steps and mandatory rinse/check procedures

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 causing underfill with no visible drips (supported by SOP cause hierarchy and work instruction); repeat‑failure history of worn seals on the same valve is a secondary lead that must be inspected.
- Difference vs. history: this is the first alarm on valve 12 without dripping; previous underfill alarms involved valves 9 and 15 with drips, and a past NCR linked valve 12 to worn seals. The three‑alarm pattern in one shift now meets the systemic‑fault trigger.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped per SOP after the third alarm; line down until nozzle cleaned and first‑bottle check passed (≈1 hour downtime).
- Safety risk: HIGH (fault requires LOTO and production stop; safety steps mandated).
- Financial impact: estimated loss of one hour of production plus potential scrap of rejected bottles (underfill rate >0.5 % for the shift).

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms in one shift trigger a systemic fault; past seal wear on valve 12 adds a repeat‑component risk, and LOTO is required.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action:
Step 1: Safety — Press STOP (normal stop), initiate LOTO per SAF‑003, wear required PPE (safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, hearing protection), and isolate the machine.
Step 2: Diagnosis — Read the checkweigher report to confirm valve 12 underfilling; visually inspect valve 12 nozzle for blockage; verify product supply pressure is between 1.5‑2.0 bar (low‑pressure alarm threshold <1.3 bar).
Step 3: Fix — If blockage is present, lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of valve 12 according to FL‑101‑SOP Section 12.1 (nozzle cleaning). If no blockage is found, inspect the seal on valve 12 for wear and replace per WI‑FL101‑001 if wear is evident.
Step 4: Verify — Perform the mandatory first‑bottle check: run the line at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml. If any out of range, repeat diagnosis/fix.
Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles already rejected by the checkweigher; record the incident, actions taken, seal kit part number (SEAL‑FV‑24), and first‑bottle results in the maintenance log.

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Implement a scheduled nozzle‑cleaning program (daily visual check, weekly deep clean) and a seal‑wear monitoring program (replace seals every 3 months or 1 500 h, whichever comes first). Update the work order system to flag valve 12 for proactive inspection after any underfill alarm.

Preventive action:
- Add a daily “nozzle visual inspection” checklist for operators.
- Configure the control system to alert when underfill alarms reach two occurrences in a shift (pre‑emptive to the three‑alarm systemic trigger).
- Review seal‑wear data weekly; if any valve approaches the service interval, replace before failure.
- Communicate the reinforced “do NOT increase fill time” rule to all operators during the next shift‑lead meeting.

Who to notify:
- Shift supervisor
- Maintenance supervisor
- Quality lead
- Engineering change control (for preventive‑action implementation)

Alarm message: "Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar"

Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill.

Causes, most common first:
  1. Supply filter blocked — clean or replace the filter (FLT-PS-10)
  2. Air in the supply line — bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
  3. Supply tank running low — check the tank level with the water
     treatment room

Immediate action:

  Step 3 — Bleed air from the supply line.
  Step 4 — Confirm the pressure is back to 1.5 to 2.0 bar.

On the night shift of 16 January 2026, FL-101 raised underfill alarms
three times: at 21:40, 23:55 and 02:10.

After each alarm the operator increased the fill time to push more water
into the bottles: first from 3.2 to 3.6 seconds, then to 3.9 seconds.

The longer fill time made most valves overflow. Water spilled onto the
bottles and the conveyor, labels were damaged at the labeller, and the
line stopped twice to clean up spillage.

---

[Source: FL-101-NCR.txt | Type: NCR | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.84]
Root cause: the seals on four fill valves (valves 7, 12, 13 and 19) were
worn out. Raising the fill time did not fix the worn seals. It hid them for
a while and made the other 20 valves overfill.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.

  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101

        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.

        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours

            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.

Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8.                 required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.

SOURCE DATA:

- FL‑101‑SOP.txt Rev 1.0 (sections 11, 12.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4) – correct response, safety steps, specifications
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt (blocked nozzle cause, seal replacement recommendation)
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt (NCR‑2026‑012 – worn seals, “do not increase fill time” rule, corrective actions)
- Knowledge Graph (verified) – underfill causes, systemic fault rule, seal part number, LOTO procedure, mandatory first‑bottle check and sanitation rinse, estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 (no dripping observed, underfill alarm triggered)
- Difference vs historical pattern: previous underfill alarms involved valves 9 and 15 with dripping; this is the first documented case for valve 12 and the first time a blocked‑nozzle cause is seen, plus three alarms in one shift triggered the systemic‑fault escalation.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped after third alarm; estimated downtime ~1 hour including cleaning, LOTO, rinse and first‑bottle check
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO and production stop)
- Financial impact: loss of production time (~1 hour) plus potential waste of underfilled bottles; exact cost not quantified in data

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms in a single shift forced a production stop and meet the “systemic fault” rule, meeting the minimum HIGH rating.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action
  Step 1: Safety — Press STOP (normal stop), then perform LOTO per SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag, verify lockout)
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Read the checkweigher report to confirm valve 12 underfilling; visually inspect valve 12 for dripping (none observed) and for nozzle blockage
  Step 3: Fix — Clean the nozzle of valve 12 following the work instruction (lock out, remove nozzle debris, re‑install)
  Step 4: Verify — Run a sanitation rinse (10 min), then perform a first‑bottle check of 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml before restarting
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced after the alarm until the first‑bottle check passes; record actions in the maintenance log
- Root cause fix (permanent solution)
  • Implement a regular (e.g., weekly) nozzle cleaning schedule for all fill valves and add a visual inspection for blockage during routine maintenance
- Preventive action (stops recurrence)
  • Add a shift‑lead check of nozzle condition when the checkweigher reject count exceeds 1 %/hour
  • Reinforce training that fill time must never be altered; update SOP reminder on the control panel
  • Track seal wear intervals and replace seals before the 1,500‑hour limit to avoid combined wear and blockage issues
- Who to notify
  • Maintenance Supervisor
  • Shift Lead
  • Quality Lead

STATUS: Line stopped; LOTO applied and cleaning in progress.  
ACTION REQUIRED: Lock out the machine, clean valve 12’s nozzle, run the mandatory rinse and first‑bottle check before restarting.  
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued underfill will force another production stop, increase downtime, and may lead to product quality loss or safety violations.

On the night shift of 16 January 2026, FL-101 raised underfill alarms
three times: at 21:40, 23:55 and 02:10.

After each alarm the operator increased the fill time to push more water
into the bottles: first from 3.2 to 3.6 seconds, then to 3.9 seconds.

The longer fill time made most valves overflow. Water spilled onto the
bottles and the conveyor, labels were damaged at the labeller, and the
line stopped twice to clean up spillage.

---

[Source: FL-101-NCR.txt | Type: NCR | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.84]
Root cause: the seals on four fill valves (valves 7, 12, 13 and 19) were
worn out. Raising the fill time did not fix the worn seals. It hid them for
a while and made the other 20 valves overfill.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  - The SOP did not say that operators must not change the fill time.
  - No spare seal kits were in stock on the line that night.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.

        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen

        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8.             time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes

            who: Trained maintenance technicians only

                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.

                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Underfill), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, SOP, NCR
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections on alarm response, underfill procedure, product supply pressure, cleaning steps, safety rules
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt – NCR‑2026‑012 (closed) – worn‑seal history on valve 12 and corrective actions
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt – underfill causes (blocked nozzle, worn seal) and replacement criteria
- DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-10-Night.csv – three underfill alarms on valve 12 in one shift
- WI‑FL101‑001 (Work Instruction) – seal‑replacement steps, LOTO, sanitation rinse, first‑bottle check
- Knowledge‑graph entry “FAULT: Underfill” – causes order, systemic rule, specifications for fill volume and fill time

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 (no dripping observed, underfill alarm) possibly compounded by prior worn‑seal history on the same valve.
- Difference from historical pattern: first time the alarm involves valve 12 without any drip; three underfill alarms occurred in a single shift, triggering the systemic‑fault rule.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped for investigation; estimated downtime ~1 hour including lock‑out, cleaning, sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO, PPE, and lock‑out before any cleaning; failure to follow could expose personnel to moving parts or product spillage).
- Financial impact: loss of production for ~1 hour plus potential reject rate increase if underfill continues; exact cost not quantified in data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – three underfill alarms in one shift meet the “systemic fault” trigger defined in the SOP and knowledge graph; a production stop and maintenance work order are required.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Press STOP (normal stop), apply LOTO per SAF‑003, wear safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, and hearing protection.
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Read the checkweigher report to confirm valve 12 underfills; lock out the machine; inspect valve 12 nozzle for blockage.
  Step 3: Fix — Clean the nozzle of valve 12 as described in SOP Section 12.1 (lock out, remove debris, re‑install); then check product supply pressure (must be 1.5–2.0 bar). If pressure is low, follow low‑pressure procedure (clean filter, bleed air, verify pressure) before restarting.
  Step 4: Verify — Perform the mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min) and then the first‑bottle check (weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495–505 ml). Do not adjust fill time under any circumstance.
  Step 5: Quality — If any bottle fails the first‑bottle check, repeat nozzle cleaning or raise a maintenance work order for seal inspection/replacement; quarantine any out‑of‑spec bottles.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): If nozzle cleaning does not resolve underfill, replace the fill‑valve seal on valve 12 using WI‑FL101‑001 (seal kit SEAL‑FV‑24) and verify seat condition; document in maintenance log.
- Preventive action: Add a weekly nozzle inspection for valves 9, 12, 15 and any valve that triggers an underfill alarm; track seal service interval (every 3 months or 1 500 h) and replace proactively; update shift lead when three underfill alarms occur in a shift.
- Who to notify: Shift supervisor, Maintenance supervisor, Quality lead, and Engineering (for seal‑service schedule review).

PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

SITUATION: Valve 12 is underfilling bottles with no drip, causing three underfill alarms in one shift.  
ROOT CAUSE: Blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 (possible recurrence of prior seal wear).  
STATUS: Line stopped; LOTO applied; cleaning in progress.  
ACTION REQUIRED: Lock out the machine, clean valve 12’s nozzle, verify product pressure, and complete the mandatory sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check before restart.  
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued underfill will increase reject rate, may trigger a production stop, and expose operators to safety hazards.

On the night shift of 16 January 2026, FL-101 raised underfill alarms
three times: at 21:40, 23:55 and 02:10.

After each alarm the operator increased the fill time to push more water
into the bottles: first from 3.2 to 3.6 seconds, then to 3.9 seconds.

The longer fill time made most valves overflow. Water spilled onto the
bottles and the conveyor, labels were damaged at the labeller, and the
line stopped twice to clean up spillage.

---

[Source: FL-101-NCR.txt | Type: NCR | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.84]
Root cause: the seals on four fill valves (valves 7, 12, 13 and 19) were
worn out. Raising the fill time did not fix the worn seals. It hid them for
a while and made the other 20 valves overfill.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]

            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)

- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑11‑Day.csv – follow‑up data (no new alarms)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Worn fill‑valve seals are dripping between fills, causing under‑fill alarms and a creeping reject count. (Evidence: SOP “early warning” and “possible causes – worn fill valve seal”; Alarm logs show three Underfill alarms in one shift; reject rate 14/1000 exceeds SOP threshold of >1/100.)
- Difference vs. history: This is the first recorded occurrence of Underfill alarms for FL‑101; previous logs showed only rising reject counts without alarms.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line is operating with elevated rejects; if trend continues a production stop will be required per SOP (3+ alarms = stop).
- Safety risk: LOW (no electrical, fire, or injury events reported; only mechanical wear).
- Financial impact: Increased reject rate (~14 per 1,000 bottles) reduces yield and may require rework or scrap; potential downtime ~1 hour for seal replacement (knowledge‑graph estimate).

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – three Underfill alarms in a single shift trigger a systemic fault and require production stop per SOP; recurring fault indicator meets HIGH minimum.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Press STOP (normal stop), apply LOTO per SAF‑003, isolate power and lock out the machine.
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Read the checkweigher report to identify under‑filling valves; inspect those valves for dripping.
  Step 3: Fix — For each valve that drips, replace the fill‑valve seal kit (SEAL‑FV‑24) following WI‑FL101‑001 steps: remove valve, remove old seal, clean seat, fit new seal with food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1, re‑install valve, remove lock, refill bowl.
  Step 4: Verify — Perform the mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min) then run first‑bottle check (first 20 bottles must be 495‑505 ml); record results and have shift supervisor sign off.
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced since the first alarm; re‑weigh a sample batch to confirm reject rate is below 1/100.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Replace all worn seals on the line and adjust the preventive‑maintenance interval to no longer than 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first; document seal condition in the maintenance log.
- Preventive action: Implement daily reject‑count monitoring; if reject count exceeds 1 per 100 bottles in any hour, notify shift lead immediately (SOP early‑warning). Add a scheduled seal‑inspection task to the maintenance calendar. Train operators to report dripping valves before alarms trigger.
- Who to notify: Shift lead, Maintenance Supervisor, Quality Lead, and Production Control.

PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

ROOT CAUSE: Worn fill‑valve seals are dripping, causing under‑fill and increased rejects.
STATUS: Line is running but at risk; a production stop is required if the trend continues.
ACTION REQUIRED: Stop the line, apply LOTO, replace the dripping valve seals, and complete the sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check before restarting.
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued rejects will exceed quality limits, leading to product scrap, possible forced line shutdown, and loss of production time.

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor
      meaning: Several worn seals: a systemic fault, not bad luck
      trigger: 3 or more underfill alarms in one shift

          electrical rule: Do not attempt electrical repairs. Always call maintenance.

SOURCE DATA:

- WI‑FL101‑001 (Work Instruction) – sections referenced in knowledge graph
- Knowledge Graph entries for FL‑101 (verified facts)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: early‑stage underfill indicated by a rising reject count (>1 % per hour) most likely due to worn fill‑valve seals or a blocked nozzle, as defined in the SOP and reinforced by past NCR‑2026‑012.
- Difference from historical pattern: this is the first occurrence of a rising reject count without a recorded underfill alarm; historically underfill alarms trigger after three consecutive rejects, but the SOP flags the reject count itself as an early warning.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line is running but product reject rate is increasing, causing degraded output and risk of further downtime.
- Safety risk: HIGH (fault requires LOTO for inspection and possible seal replacement; safety rules mandate lock‑out before any maintenance).
- Financial impact: potential loss from rejected product and possible overtime for corrective maintenance; exact dollar amount not determinable from provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Justification: fault requires LOTO, involves components with a documented NCR history of wear, and the SOP treats a reject count >1 %/hour as a warning that can progress to systemic underfill if unaddressed.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Press STOP (normal stop), then perform LOTO as per SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start).
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Read the checkweigher report to identify which fill valves are under‑filling; inspect each flagged valve for dripping.
  Step 3: Fix — 
    - If a valve is dripping, replace its seal kit (WI‑FL101‑001) following the documented seal‑replacement steps.
    - If no dripping, lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the under‑filling valve.
    - After any seal work, verify product supply pressure is ≥ 1.3 bar.
  Step 4: Verify — Perform the mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min) then run the first‑bottle check (weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml). Record results and obtain shift‑supervisor sign‑off.
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced since the reject count began; re‑weigh a sample batch to confirm reject rate is back below 1 % per hour.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution):
  Replace any worn seals identified, clean blocked nozzles, and adjust the maintenance interval if more than four seals are found worn before the 3‑month/1,500‑hour limit.

- Preventive action:
  - Implement hourly reject‑count monitoring; if >1 % per hour, automatically raise a maintenance work order.
  - Enforce the SOP rule that three underfill alarms in a shift trigger a production stop and escalation.
  - Review seal‑stock levels to ensure at least 10 kits are on hand; schedule preventive seal replacement at the 3‑month or 1,500‑hour interval regardless of alarm history.
  - Provide a brief refresher to operators on the “do NOT increase fill time” rule.

- Who to notify:
  Shift lead, Maintenance Supervisor, Quality Lead, and Plant Manager.

═══════════════════════════════════════
PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

SITUATION: Reject count is rising above the 1 % per hour threshold with no alarms yet.  
ROOT CAUSE: Early‑stage underfill likely caused by worn fill‑valve seals or a blocked nozzle.  
STATUS: Line is still running but at risk of increased rejects and possible shutdown.  
ACTION REQUIRED: Stop the line, lock out, inspect the checkweigher report, and replace any leaking seals or clean blocked nozzles per SOP.  
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued reject growth could trigger systemic underfill, force an unscheduled production stop, and lead to significant product loss.

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]

- Knowledge‑graph entry for FL‑101 (verified facts from SOP, WI‑FL101‑001, NCR)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: early‑stage underfill due to worn fill‑valve seals, indicated by a rising reject count that has not yet triggered the underfill alarm threshold. (evidence: SOP early‑warning rule, alarm agent pattern of underfill caused by dripping valves, NCR‑2026‑012 seal wear history)
- Difference from historical pattern: previous incidents produced immediate underfill alarms; this occurrence shows only a gradual increase in rejects before any alarm, suggesting the fault is developing but not yet meeting the “3 underfill alarms in one shift” trigger.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line continues running but with elevated reject rate (≈ 14 / 1,000), leading to degraded output and increased scrap.
- Safety risk: LOW (no LOTO required yet, no electrical or fire hazard reported).
- Financial impact: increased waste cost proportional to reject rate; exact dollar amount not calculable from provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- MEDIUM – rising reject count is an early warning of a systemic underfill fault; it does not yet meet the HIGH criteria of three alarms or a production stop, but it can lead to HIGH if left unchecked.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety – Press the normal STOP button, then apply LOTO per SAF‑003 before any inspection or maintenance.
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Read the checkweigher report to identify which valve(s) are under‑filling.
  Step 3: Fix – 
    - If the identified valve is dripping, replace its seal kit (SEAL‑FV‑24) following WI‑FL101‑001 steps.
    - If no drip is observed, lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the under‑filling valve (SOP Section 12.1).
    - After seal work or cleaning, verify product supply pressure is ≥ 1.3 bar (SOP Section 12.4).
  Step 4: Verify – Perform the mandatory sanitation rinse, then run a first‑bottle check of 20 bottles; all must be within 495‑505 ml before restart.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine any out‑of‑spec bottles, record the reject count, and update the maintenance log with seal‑kit part number, valve number, and operator name.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution):
  Replace all worn fill‑valve seals that have reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours, and adjust the preventive‑maintenance interval if multiple seals are found worn early.

- Preventive action:
  • Monitor reject count hourly; if > 1 / 100 over an hour, stop the line and follow the above inspection procedure.
  • Add a daily check of the checkweigher trend to the shift‑lead checklist.
  • Ensure seal replacement is performed at the documented 3‑month/1,500‑hour interval; consider shortening interval if wear recurs.
  • Retrain operators on the early‑warning reject‑count rule and the prohibition on increasing fill time.

- Who to notify:
  Shift supervisor, Maintenance supervisor, Quality Lead, and Engineering (for interval review).

            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

═══════════════════════════════════════
INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Infeed Jam), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv (alarm events)
- FL-101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 8.2, 9, 10, 12.2, 14
- FL-101‑Work‑Instruction.txt (seal replacement instructions)
- Knowledge‑Graph entry for FL‑101 (specifications, safety rules, changeover steps)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Valve leakage (valves 9, 15, 3) after a changeover to 330 ml bottles, combined with the absence of a documented changeover procedure for the 330 ml size, allowed the leak to go unchecked and caused three Underfill alarms in one night shift. (Evidence: Alarm Agent – 3 underfill alarms linked to valve leakage; SOP gap – no 330 ml changeover procedure)
- Difference vs historical pattern: This is the first recorded underfill alarm for FL‑101; previous logs show only infeed jams. The recurrence of three alarms in a single shift meets the “three‑or‑more” trigger for a HIGH‑severity fault. (Evidence: Alarm Agent – “first documented instance”; Knowledge‑Graph – trigger rule for 3+ same‑type alarms)

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line stopped for each alarm; repeated stops degraded output and risked missing shift target.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO for any valve inspection/replacement; underfill itself is not a direct safety hazard but the required lockout and potential exposure to leaking product elevate risk)
- Financial impact: Not quantified in data; implied loss from downtime and potential scrap of underfilled bottles.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Three underfill alarms in one shift trigger the HIGH‑severity rule; LOTO is required for valve work, raising the criticality to at least HIGH.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action:
Step 1: Safety — LOTO the fill line per SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag, verify power off) and wear required PPE (safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses). (Source: Knowledge‑Graph, FL‑101‑SOP §6.2, §6.1)
Step 2: Diagnosis — 
- Inspect valves 9, 15, 3 for leakage or seal wear. 
- Verify guide rail position matches the 330 ml specification (Rail position B) and that the star wheel is correctly fitted. (Source: Knowledge‑Graph §8.2, §14)
Step 3: Fix —
- Replace any leaking valve seals using the seal‑replacement work instruction. 
- Re‑set guide rails to position B and lock them. 
- Re‑fit the matching star wheel. (Source: Knowledge‑Graph changeover steps §14)
Step 4: Verify —
- Remove LOTO, restart machine at 60 bottles per minute, run at least 20 bottles and measure fill level; ensure no underfill alarm for a minimum of 30 minutes. 
- Return line speed to normal (≤130 bpm) after verification. (Source: Knowledge‑Graph §9‑§10)
Step 5: Quality —
- Quarantine any bottles produced during the alarm periods; inspect for underfill and discard or rework per quality policy. (Derived from standard quality practice)

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Develop and publish a detailed 330 ml changeover SOP that includes valve seal inspection, guide‑rail verification, and post‑changeover fill‑level test before returning to full speed.

Preventive action:
- Add valve‑leak check to the changeover checklist. 
- Schedule periodic preventive maintenance on fill valves (seal replacement interval per work instruction). 
- Train all operators on the new 330 ml changeover SOP and require sign‑off in the shift log. 
- Implement a “first‑hour post‑changeover” fill‑level verification step.

Who to notify:
- Shift Lead, Maintenance Supervisor, Quality Lead, and the Process Engineering team.

═══════════════════════════════════════
PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

SITUATION: Three underfill alarms occurred on the night shift after an undocumented changeover to 330 ml bottles.  
ROOT CAUSE: Leaking fill valves were not inspected because no SOP exists for the 330 ml changeover.  
STATUS: Line is stopped pending LOTO, valve inspection, and corrective actions.  
ACTION REQUIRED: Implement LOTO, inspect/replace leaking valve seals, and verify fill level before restarting.  
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued underfill alarms will cause repeated line stops, product loss, and possible safety violations due to un‑locked equipment.

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Infeed Jam), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- Infeed jam alarm during 330 ml changeover, DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-07-Day.csv (2026‑09‑07 Day shift) – HIGH confidence
- Infeed Jam safety rule – “Never reach into the infeed … Stop the machine and lock it out before clearing any jam.” FL-101-SOP Section 12.2 – TIER 1 VERIFIED
- Guide Rail Setting specification – Rail position B for 330 ml, rails locked, matching star wheel fitted. FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2 and 14 – TIER 1 VERIFIED
- Line Speed specification – start at 60 bpm, then raise to normal 120 bpm. FL-101-SOP Sections 9 and 10 – TIER 1 VERIFIED
- Infeed Jam causes list – 1) Guide rails not reset after changeover; 2) Chipped/damaged bottles; 3) Conveyor too fast. FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2, 12.2, 14 – TIER 1 VERIFIED
- Infeed Jam Clearing procedure steps (1‑6). FL-101-SOP Section 12.2 – TIER 1 VERIFIED
- LOTO (SAF‑003) steps – switch off power, lock isolator, tag, verify. FL-101-SOP Section 6.2 – TIER 1 VERIFIED
- SOP gap – no detailed procedure for swapping to 330 ml after lunch. FL-101‑SOP.txt Revision 1.0 – TIER 2 DOCUMENTS (LOW confidence)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Guide rails were not reset to the 330 ml position after the lunch changeover, leading to an infeed jam. (Supported by knowledge‑graph cause list and “most infeed jams in the first hour after a changeover come from rails left in the wrong position.”)
- Difference from historical pattern: This is the first recorded alarm associated with a 330 ml changeover; previous 330 ml runs logged without jams. The lack of a documented post‑lunch changeover procedure contributed to the deviation.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line stopped for jam clearance; reduced output until jam cleared and line restarted at reduced speed.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO and PPE; jam clearing involves reaching into machine area).
- Financial impact: Not quantified in provided data; implied loss from downtime and potential scrap.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – fault requires LOTO and production stop; recurring‑fault indicator (first of a potential series) and aligns with mandatory safety rule that any maintenance or jam clearing must be locked out.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action (reproduce approved steps verbatim):
Step 1: Press STOP.  
Step 2: Lock out the machine – follow LOTO (SAF‑003): 1) Switch off power at the main isolator. 2) Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3) Tag it with your name and the date. 4) Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.  
Step 3: Remove the jammed bottles wearing cut‑resistant gloves.  
Step 4: Check the guide rail position matches the 330 ml bottle size (Rail position B) and reset the rails if they are wrong; lock the rails and fit the matching star wheel.  
Step 5: Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed.  
Step 6: Remove the lock, restart at 60 bottles per minute for 2 minutes, then return to normal speed (120 bpm); record the changeover in the shift log and have the shift lead sign the record.

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Implement and train on the documented “Bottle Size Changeover” procedure (FL‑101‑SOP Section 14) for all post‑lunch changeovers, ensuring guide rails are set to position B and locked before restart.

Preventive action (stops recurrence):
- Add the changeover steps to the shift‑lead checklist and update the SOP to include a specific “Swap to 330 ml after lunch” work instruction.
- Conduct a short refresher on LOTO and guide‑rail verification for all operators before the next shift change.
- Log every changeover in the shift record and audit compliance

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Infeed Jam), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-07-Day.csv – alarm record for 330 ml change‑over with infeed jam (two occurrences)
- DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-08-Day.csv – no 330 ml change‑over alarm
- DemoBottling-Shift-Log-2026-09-10-Night.csv – single 330 ml change‑over alarm after lunch (current incident)
- FL-101-SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – sections 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 8.2, 9, 10, 12.2, 14 (guide‑rail specs, LOTO, safety rules, changeover steps)
- FL-101-Work-Instruction.txt – seal‑replacement instructions (used only to confirm no relevant maintenance record)
- Knowledge‑graph entry “Guide Rail Setting – bottle 330 ml: Rail position B” (source: FL-101‑SOP Sections 8.2 & 14)
- Knowledge‑graph entry “Changeover procedure steps” (source: FL-101‑SOP Section 14)
- Knowledge‑graph entry “LOTO (SAF‑003) requirements” (source: FL-101‑SOP Section 6.2)
- Knowledge‑graph entry “Machine Safety Rules” (source: FL-101‑SOP Sections 6.3 & 6.4)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Guide rails were not reset to the 330 ml position (Rail B) after the post‑lunch change‑over, triggering the change‑over alarm. (Evidence: SOP specification for rail position B and “first check” rule in knowledge graph; alarm log shows first‑time occurrence after a change‑over.)
- Difference from historical pattern: This is the first recorded 330 ml change‑over alarm without an accompanying infeed jam; previous 330 ml change‑over on 2026‑09‑07 included jam alarms. (Evidence: Alarm agent low‑confidence log analysis.)

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line stopped for change‑over; downtime until guide rails are correctly set and machine restarted.
- Safety risk: HIGH (LOTO required; any jam or broken bottle could cause injury; safety rules mandate lockout before any adjustment).
- Financial impact: Estimated loss of one shift’s output (~120 bpm × 8 h ≈ 57,600 bottles) plus labor cost for lockout and re‑start.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Justification: Fault requires LOTO and production stop; safety rules mandate lockout before any adjustment, meeting the HIGH minimum threshold.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Apply LOTO (SAF‑003): switch off power at main isolator, place personal padlock, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start.
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Verify change‑over record is signed; inspect guide rail position and confirm it matches Rail B for 330 ml bottles; ensure rails are locked and correct star wheel is fitted.
  Step 3: Fix — Reset guide rails to Rail B per change‑over sheet CS‑FL101; lock rails; fit matching star wheel.
  Step 4: Verify — Remove LOTO, start machine at 60 bpm, run 20 bottles, observe for jams; if clear, ramp to normal speed (120 bpm) and monitor first 2 minutes.
  Step 5: Quality — Inspect first 20 bottles for fill quality; quarantine any defective bottles; record results in shift log and have shift lead sign the change‑over record.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Formalize the post‑lunch 330 ml change‑over procedure in the FL‑101 SOP, including mandatory guide‑rail verification and LOTO steps.
- Preventive action: Train all operators on the updated SOP; add a checklist item for “Guide rail set to position B” on the change‑over sheet; schedule a quarterly audit of change‑over records.
