12.1 Underfill
Alarm message: "Fill level low — bottles under target volume"
The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row.

This is the most common alarm on FL-101. Causes, most common first:
  1. Worn fill valve seal — the valve drips between fills
  2. Blocked fill nozzle — debris in the nozzle, no dripping
  3. Low product supply pressure — see Section 12.4

---

[Source: FL-101-SOP.txt | Type: SOP | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.84]
Immediate action:
  Step 1 — Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone
           is in danger).
  Step 2 — Read the checkweigher report. It shows which valve numbers are
           underfilling.
  Step 3 — Look at those valves. Dripping means a worn seal: call the
           maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using work
           instruction WI-FL101-001.
  Step 4 — No dripping: lock out the machine (Section 6.2) and clean the
           nozzle of that valve.
  Step 5 — Check the product supply pressure (Section 12.4).

Do NOT increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn
seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012).

Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually
several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and
call the maintenance supervisor.

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Improper seal installation or damaged valve seat on the recently serviced fill valve, producing a side leak rather than a nozzle drip. Evidence: seal kit was replaced “yesterday” (operator report) but no maintenance record exists; knowledge graph defines side‑leak symptom as a sign of seal or seat failure.

- Production impact: Line stopped for leak repair; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour (LOTO, seal/valve work, sanitation rinse, first‑bottle check).

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action:
Step 1: Safety — Activate LOTO per SAF‑003: switch off main power, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start.
Step 2: Diagnosis — Visually inspect the leaking valve for side‑leak path; confirm seal is seated correctly and valve seat is not scratched or cracked.
Step 3: Fix — 
  - If seal is mis‑installed or damaged, re‑perform seal replacement using WI‑FL101‑001 steps 1‑10. 
  - If valve seat is scratched, replace the valve (or seat) per maintenance guidelines; document in maintenance log.
Step 4: Verify — 
  - Perform mandatory sanitation rinse (WI‑FL101‑001 Step 9). 
  - Conduct first‑bottle check of 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml.

Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any product produced after the leak until first‑bottle check passes; record results and sign‑off by shift supervisor.

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Reinforce seal installation verification after any seal change (add a post‑maintenance visual check and torque verification if applicable) and replace any valve with damaged seat.

Preventive action:
- Update maintenance work order to include a “side‑leak inspection” checklist after seal changes. 
- Train technicians on correct seal seating and seat inspection. 
- Review and, if needed, tighten the 1,500‑hour/3‑month seal‑change interval compliance audit.

This work instruction explains how to replace the seal kit in an FL-101
fill valve. A worn seal is the most common cause of underfill alarms.

8. PROCEDURE

  Step 1 — Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO).
  Step 2 — Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level.
  Step 3 — Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left).
  Step 4 — Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick.
  Step 5 — Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth. Check it for
           scratches. A scratched seat must be reported to the maintenance
           supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat.
  Step 6 — Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit, with a thin
           layer of FGL-1 lubricant.
  Step 7 — Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks).
  Step 8 — Count the tools and parts on the tray. Remove the lock and refill
           the bowl.

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor
      meaning: Several worn seals: a systemic fault, not bad luck
      trigger: 3 or more underfill alarms in one shift

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: side leak of the fill valve indicates a worn or improperly installed seal (knowledge graph, SOP, work instruction). The seal was replaced yesterday, but the leak persists, suggesting either a defective seal kit or incorrect installation.
- Difference vs historical pattern: this is the first recorded under‑fill alarm for FL‑101 in the supplied logs; no prior recurring alarms or repeat failures on the same valve are documented.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line is at risk of stoppage; expected downtime for proper repair ≈ 1 hour (estimated in knowledge graph) plus any additional time if repeat leak occurs.
- Safety risk: LOW (no injury or hazardous material involved) but LOTO is required for the repair.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – fault requires LOTO and a production stop to replace the seal; recurring under‑fill alarms would trigger a systemic fault (criticality rule). No safety‑critical event is present, but the need for lockout and possible production loss sets the rating at HIGH.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety – Press STOP (normal stop), then perform LOTO as defined in SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify lockout).
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Read the checkweigher report to confirm which valve is under‑filling; visually inspect the side of the identified valve for dripping.
  Step 3: Fix – Call the maintenance technician and replace the seal kit (SEAL‑FV‑24) using WI‑FL101‑001:
    1. Drain the bowl below valve level.
    2. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn left).
    3. Remove old seal and O‑ring with seal pick.
    4. Clean valve seat; inspect for scratches (report if scratched).
    5. Fit new seal and O‑ring with a thin layer of food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1.
    6. Re‑install valve (quarter turn right until click).
    7. Remove lock, refill bowl.
  Step 4: Verify – Perform mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min clean water) then conduct First‑Bottle Check (weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml). Do not adjust fill time.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine any bottles produced after the leak until First‑Bottle Check passes; record seal part number, technician name, date, and checkweigher results in the maintenance log.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Ensure seal installation follows the documented procedure, verify seal part number (SEAL‑FV‑24) and condition before installation, and add a post‑install visual inspection sign‑off by the technician.

- Preventive action:
  - Add a verification step in the seal‑change work instruction: technician must confirm no side drip before releasing LOTO.
  - Schedule seal inspections at the 1,500‑hour interval and after any seal change.
  - Stock minimum 10 seal kits (as per specification) and track usage in the maintenance log.
  - Conduct a short refresher training for maintenance staff on the LOTO and seal‑replacement steps.
  - Update the shift lead checklist to include “visual check for side leak after seal change”.

1. PURPOSE

This work instruction explains how to replace the seal kit in an FL-101
fill valve. A worn seal is the most common cause of underfill alarms.

2. SCOPE

Applies to all 24 fill valves on the FL-101 Bottle Filler. Only trained
maintenance technicians may carry out this work.

[Source: FL-101-Work-Instruction.txt | Type: Work Instruction | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.83]
8. PROCEDURE

  Step 1 — Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO).
  Step 2 — Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level.
  Step 3 — Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left).
  Step 4 — Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick.
  Step 5 — Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth. Check it for
           scratches. A scratched seat must be reported to the maintenance
           supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat.
  Step 6 — Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit, with a thin
           layer of FGL-1 lubricant.
  Step 7 — Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks).
  Step 8 — Count the tools and parts on the tray. Remove the lock and refill
           the bowl.

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: side leak of the fill valve caused by a worn or improperly seated seal (as defined in SOP and confirmed by repeat‑failure NCR) despite seals being replaced yesterday.
- Difference from historical pattern: this is the first underfill alarm recorded in the supplied shift logs, but it matches the known repeat failure mode (worn seals) documented in NCR‑2026‑012.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line operating under underfill condition; if additional alarms occur the line must be stopped per SOP (estimated downtime ~1 hour for seal replacement and first‑bottle check).
- Safety risk: HIGH (fault requires LOTO for inspection/replacement; LOTO is mandatory safety step).
- Financial impact: potential loss from off‑spec product and downtime; exact cost not quantified in provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Justification: fault requires LOTO and is a repeat failure mode documented in a closed NCR; three‑plus alarms would trigger a production stop, so the minimum rating is HIGH.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — Equip PPE (safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, hearing protection). Press STOP, then perform LOTO per SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify lockout).
  Step 2: Diagnosis — Drain bowl below valve level, remove valve, inspect side of valve for leak, check seal condition and valve seat for scratches or damage.
  Step 3: Fix — If seal is worn or seat is scratched:
    • Replace seal kit SEAL‑FV‑24 using WI‑FL101‑001 steps 1‑8 (apply food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1, fit new seal, re‑install valve).
    • If seat is scratched, report to Maintenance Supervisor and schedule seat replacement; do not reinstall seal on a damaged seat.
  Step 4: Verify — Perform mandatory sanitation rinse (10 min clean water) then conduct first‑bottle check (weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml). Shift supervisor signs off.
  Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles outside spec, record seal‑change details (date, valve number, part number, technician name) in maintenance log, and update underfill alarm log.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution):
  • Reinforce seal‑installation training for maintenance technicians.
  • Add a post‑replacement seat‑inspection step to WI‑FL101‑001.
  • Adjust preventive‑maintenance interval to no more than 1,500 h or 3 months, whichever is earlier, and track seal life in the maintenance log.

- Preventive action:
  • Implement a daily checkweigher trend review; if underfill trend appears, raise a work order before three alarms occur.
  • Stock minimum of 10 seal kits (as per part data) and conduct a quarterly audit of seal inventory.
  • Update SOP to highlight “do NOT increase fill time” warning (already present) and circulate reminder to all operators.

- Who to notify:
  • Shift Supervisor
  • Maintenance Supervisor
  • Quality Lead
  • Engineering (for review of seal‑installation procedure)

1. PURPOSE

This work instruction explains how to replace the seal kit in an FL-101
fill valve. A worn seal is the most common cause of underfill alarms.

2. SCOPE

Applies to all 24 fill valves on the FL-101 Bottle Filler. Only trained
maintenance technicians may carry out this work.

[Source: FL-101-Work-Instruction.txt | Type: Work Instruction | Revision: 1.0 | Score: 0.83]
8. PROCEDURE

  Step 1 — Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO).
  Step 2 — Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level.
  Step 3 — Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left).
  Step 4 — Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick.
  Step 5 — Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth. Check it for
           scratches. A scratched seat must be reported to the maintenance
           supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat.
  Step 6 — Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit, with a thin
           layer of FGL-1 lubricant.
  Step 7 — Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks).
  Step 8 — Count the tools and parts on the tray. Remove the lock and refill
           the bowl.

        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.

        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen

        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped

            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes

  - The seal has reached its limit: 3 months or 1,500 running hours,

- Difference vs. history: Previous events triggered audible under‑fill alarms after valve drip; the current event shows a gradual rise in rejects with no alarm, indicating the fault is now manifesting as a quality drift rather than an immediate alarm condition.

- Production impact: Line is running but reject rate is climbing, reducing effective output and increasing re‑work/ scrap.

- HIGH
- Justification: Three under‑fill alarms occurred in one shift (night shift 2026‑09‑10) meeting the “three‑or‑more alarms” rule, and the current quality drift could soon trigger a line stop if rejects exceed tolerance.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action (numbered steps – safety first):
Step 1: Safety — Initiate LOTO on FL‑101 Bottle Filler and stop the line to prevent further rejects.
Step 2: Diagnosis — Inspect filler seals for wear or damage; verify valve seating on valves 9, 15, and 3 for drip.
Step 3: Fix — If seals are worn, replace them per FL‑101 Work Instruction; clean or repair any dripping valves identified.
Step 4: Verify — Run a test batch, measure fill time (target 3.2 s per NCR‑2026‑012) and confirm reject rate returns to <0.5 %.
Step 5: Quality — Quarantine any bottles produced since the reject count began; re‑inspect and disposition according to QA policy.

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Implement a preventive seal‑inspection interval tied to running hours and any under‑fill alarm, and replace seals before the 3‑month/1,500‑hour limit is reached.

Preventive action (stops recurrence):
- Add a daily reject‑rate trend check to shift logs; trigger a maintenance work order when reject rate exceeds 0.5 % for two consecutive checks.
- Record all seal‑replacement activities in the maintenance log to close the documentation gap identified.

- Production Supervisor, Maintenance Lead, Quality Assurance Manager, and Engineering Change Control.

- Production impact: line continues running but reject rate ↑ (~14 per 1,000), leading to scrap and potential downstream quality hold.

- Financial impact: increased scrap cost proportional to reject volume; exact dollar amount not determinable from provided data.

- HIGH – three under‑fill alarms occurred in a single shift on 2026‑09‑10 (recurring fault indicator) and the same failure mode is now manifesting as a rising reject count.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety — LOTO FL‑101, stop the bottle filler, isolate power and pneumatic supply.
  Step 2: Diagnosis — inspect valves 9, 15, 3 for leakage; verify seal condition against work‑instruction criteria.
  Step 3: Fix — replace any leaking valve seals or the entire valve as required; reset fill time to 3.2 s per NCR‑2026‑012 corrective action.
  Step 4: Verify — run a test batch, monitor fill volume, confirm reject count returns to baseline and that no under‑fill alarm triggers.
  Step 5: Quality — quarantine any bottles produced during the fault period; perform a visual inspection of the batch.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution): install new valve seals (or replace faulty valves) and recalibrate fill‑time settings; update valve maintenance log.

- Preventive action (stops recurrence):
  • Add a daily reject‑trend check to shift start‑up SOP; trigger LOTO if reject rate exceeds 10 per 1,000 before an alarm.
  • Schedule preventive seal replacement per work‑instruction (every 3 months or 1,500 hrs) and log completion.
  • Review alarm threshold settings to ensure earlier detection of under‑fill trends.

8. PROCEDURE

  Step 1 — Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO).
  Step 2 — Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level.
  Step 3 — Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left).
  Step 4 — Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick.
  Step 5 — Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth. Check it for
           scratches. A scratched seat must be reported to the maintenance
           supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat.
  Step 6 — Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit, with a thin
           layer of FGL-1 lubricant.
  Step 7 — Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks).
  Step 8 — Count the tools and parts on the tray. Remove the lock and refill
           the bowl.

1. PURPOSE

This work instruction explains how to replace the seal kit in an FL-101
fill valve. A worn seal is the most common cause of underfill alarms.

2. SCOPE

maintenance technicians may carry out this work.

8. PROCEDURE

  Step 1 — Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO).
  Step 2 — Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level.
  Step 3 — Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left).
  Step 4 — Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick.
  Step 5 — Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth. Check it for
           scratches. A scratched seat must be reported to the maintenance
           supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat.
  Step 6 — Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit, with a thin
           layer of FGL-1 lubricant.
  Step 7 — Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks).
  Step 8 — Count the tools and parts on the tray. Remove the lock and refill
           the bowl.
